# An automated migration changes generated code through its generator and regenerates the output without hand-editing the generated files

## Thesis
When an automated migration reaches a file that carries a generated-code marker (a header comment placed before the file's first non-comment, non-blank text, or an annotation on a generated declaration, that conveys to humans and machine tools that the code is generated), the fix goes to the logic of the generator that produces the file and the generator is run again to update its output; the marked file, or for an annotation the annotated declaration, receives no edit of its own. When a build script generates the code at compile time and that code no longer works after the migration, the migration changes the build script by hand so that it generates compatible code.

## Rationale
A rewriting tool can recognise the marker and skip every fix whose edits touch a generated file, because the appropriate fix in that case is to the logic of the generator itself; a migration driven by such a tool leaves each marked file as it was, so the change belongs in the generator's logic. A generator invoked through a generate directive is never run automatically by the build or the tests and has to be run explicitly, so a change to its logic reaches the generated files only when the generator is run again. Code that a build script generates at compile time is an area where automated fixes cannot apply at all, and its fix is made by hand in the build script.

## Example
```typescript
bad:  // user-client.ts: Code generated by client-gen. DO NOT EDIT. @generated
      export function getUser(id: string): Promise<User> { ... } // hand-migrated
good: // client-gen/emit.ts: the generator, run again after this edit
      export const emitGetter = (type: string): string =>
        `export function get${type}(id: string): Promise<${type}> { ... }`;
```

## Limits
A file without a generated-code marker carries no signal that it is generated, so the marker grep does not reach it even when a program wrote it. An edit to the generator's own logic is the rule followed, and a marked file whose diff is the output of the generator run again in the same change is compliant. Code that a build script generates at compile time is outside the reach of automated fixes; there the rule is met by a hand change to the build script that makes it generate compatible code. Triggers match added lines only, so a finder reaches this rule when an added line carries a marker: a marked file the change adds, a header or annotation line it rewrites, or a generator or template line that prints the marker. A hand edit inside an existing generated file whose header the change leaves untouched carries no marker on an added line and does not reach the finder through these triggers. A template or boilerplate file that carries the marker text for the generator to emit is part of the generator, and an edit to it is the rule followed. A temporary edit to a generated file, such as logging added while debugging or a trial of a change before it moves into the generator, is outside the rule, which governs the edit that lands.

## Validator
Grep the hunk's file for a generated-code marker: a comment before its first non-comment, non-blank text that contains `DO NOT EDIT` or `@generated`, or an annotation whose name ends in `Generated` on a declaration, which marks that declaration only, so count only the hunks inside it. Skip a file the generator reads rather than writes, such as a template, a header boilerplate or generator source that prints the marker as text: it is part of the generator, and an edit to it is the rule followed. When the file carries one, open the change's file list and find the generator that produces the file, named in the marker, in a generate directive or in the build configuration. Trace whether the marked file's hunks are what that generator emits when run again: the same change edits the generator, its template or its input, or the hunks regenerate the file after a generator change that landed earlier, such as in another shard of the same migration. Confirm from the change description or its other hunks that the change applies a migration's rewrite, one shard of a migration included; a hand edit outside a migration is outside this rule. Validator question: **Does this migration change edit a file that carries a generated-code marker with hunks that are not the output of its generator run again?** Yes → flag.

## Finding output
When the validator answers yes, the finder emits one finding (`rule_id: CHG-27`, severity minor, `file`, `symbol`, `code` = the marker line quoted from the file and the edited lines of the generated file quoted verbatim from the diff, `fix` = the same change made in the generator's source or template, in the generator's language, followed by running the generator again, `rationale` = names the marker, the generator that owns the file and the skipping of fixes to generated files by rewriting tools).

- golang/tools `internal/analysis/driverutil/fix.go`, `ApplyFixes`: "Skip a fix if any of its edits touch a generated file."; "skipped %s that would edit generated files", logged only under `if verbose` (fetched)

(fetched)
- openjdk/jdk `src/java.compiler/share/classes/javax/annotation/processing/Generated.java`: "The Generated annotation is used to mark source code that has been generated. It can also be used to differentiate user written code from generated code in a single file." (fetched)
- rust-lang/rustfmt `Configurations.md`, §'`format_generated_files`': "A file is considered generated if any of the first several lines contain a `@generated` comment marker." (fetched)
- protocolbuffers/protobuf `src/google/protobuf/compiler/python/generator.cc`: "# Generated by the protocol buffer compiler.  DO NOT EDIT!" (fetched)
- golang/tools `gopls/internal/server/text_synchronization.go`, `warnAboutModifyingGeneratedFiles`: "Warn the user that they are editing a generated file, but don't try to stop them: there are often good reasons to do so, such as adding temporary logging, or evaluating changes to the generated code without the trouble of modifying the generator logic" (fetched)
- Caveat: the sources document two toolchains' migration tools and two ecosystems' markers; only one tool's driver is documented to skip fixes that touch marked files, and the formatter that documents `@generated` reformats marked files unless configured otherwise.
